name: PT. Terregra Asia Energy Tbk

frontmatter.title: Terregra Asia Energy — a hydro pipeline nobody has funded, priced as if it were funded
frontmatter.summary: A suspended, pre-revenue mini-hydro developer whose asset base is construction work in progress carried at IDR177.7bn against current liabilities of IDR150.4bn, most of them owed to related parties. We value the equity on reported book at a peer multiple less a liquidity discount: target Rp9.8, -63.8% — SELL. Untradeable and not actionable.
thesis: The company has never funded a plant: zero revenue since FY2024, a going-concern qualification in the FY2025 audit, and COD targets for the PPA-backed projects that have slipped repeatedly since listing.

The balance sheet is the business: assets under construction of IDR177.7bn — land, buildings and capitalised costs, not land alone — of which the directly held land line is only IDR0.9bn, against current liabilities of IDR150.4bn and a non-trade related-party payable of IDR98.8bn.
We value the equity on reported book at a peer P/BV of 1.1x and apply the house liquidity discount of 30.0% once; the target sits far below the suspended print and today's price is not a valuation.

Sisira is the one real asset: it reached Financing Date on 22 April 2022 and its COD is being re-determined for transmission readiness, with a CRS convertible ceiling of IDR199.3bn secured over the three most advanced projects. That is the strongest bull fact in the file.

Control is encumbered: CRS holds a pledge over the president director's shares and a conversion right into the PPA subsidiaries, so the price of the announced placement is not the controller's alone to set.
The DCF values the operating business at nil — no revenue, no funded capex, no COD we can underwrite — and it is carried at a residual weight only to state that conclusion rather than assume it.

catalysts.event: Completion or abandonment of the announced private placement (PMTHMETD) with the consortium that signed an investment agreement in September 2026
IDX decision on the potential delisting of the shares; trading remains suspended at the last price
Filing of the FY2026 audited accounts — a second consecutive late filing would remove any remaining listing argument

blocks.text: **SELL — target Rp9.8 versus Rp27, a return of -63.8%; and the note is academic because the shares cannot be traded.** Terregra Asia Energy is a listed Indonesian hydro developer that has never commissioned a plant. It earned no revenue in FY2024 and none in FY2025 [S5], owns no operating generating asset, and four of its five PPA-backed mini-hydro projects have never reached financial close [S5]. The exception is Sisira, which reached Financing Date in 2022 and whose COD is being re-determined by the offtaker rather than forfeited [S5]. The FY2025 audit carries a going-concern material uncertainty, an accumulated deficit of IDR-272.4bn and current liabilities exceeding current assets by IDR150.4bn [S5]. The shares have been suspended since 23 June 2025 at Rp27 [S6], sit on IDX's potential-delisting list [S2], and produced no traded volume at all over the last three months [S0].

What the market is being asked to pay is a market capitalisation of IDR74.2bn for parent equity of IDR38.5bn at the last audited date [S5] — about 1.9x book for a company whose book is construction work in progress that has already been written down once. We do not think book is the right anchor for a going concern, because the liabilities stack includes a non-trade payable to related parties of IDR98.8bn that ranks ahead of the equity and that we do not assume will be forgiven [S5]. But book, marked to what the market itself pays for comparable Indonesian power equity, is the most defensible anchor we can build from public filings, and even that anchor sits far below the suspended price.

There are three things that move the value. First, whether the private placement announced in September 2026 completes. An investment agreement between the controlling shareholder and a consortium of two Indonesian companies covers an initial cash injection through a rights-issue-exempt placement (PMTHMETD) and a "strategic agreement to create revenue" for the company [S2]. If it completes, the equity becomes a diluted claim on a funded platform; if it does not, the company runs out of cash. Second, whether the PLN purchase agreements survive. PLN drew three performance guarantees on 15 May 2025 and charged IDR8.3bn of claim fees in FY2025 [S5, S6], and the directors state that maintaining the agreements was a 2025 priority pending equity from a strategic partner [S6]. Third, what the construction work in progress is worth if it is never completed: the key audit matter states that if construction stops, the capitalised costs become an investment loss and that the loss is significant [S5].

Indonesia's power sector is a single-buyer market in which an independent producer's economics are set by its PLN tariff, its capacity factor and its ability to finance construction before it earns a rupiah. Small hydro projects are capital-intensive, site-specific and slow to permit; the developers that succeed are the ones that reach financial close early in the PPA life, because the tariff is fixed in nominal terms while construction costs are not. A developer that reaches commercial operation more than a decade after signing has usually already lost the economics to escalation and to the lender's view of the sponsor.

Terregra Asia Energy is an independent power producer in name and a project developer in fact. The group develops, builds and intends to operate run-of-river hydro and, historically, solar projects in Indonesia; the listed entity is the holding company of a set of project special-purpose vehicles, each holding land, permits and, for five of them, a power purchase agreement with the North Sumatra distribution unit of PLN [S5]. The company describes itself on its own website as the first Indonesian company focused on developing renewable energy, with an ambition of several hundred megawatts of operating capacity within a few years of listing [S3] — a target that was not met and that the current filings no longer repeat.

The portfolio is best described in two tiers. The first tier is five mini-hydro plants (PLTMH) with a combined capacity of 43.8 MW that hold PPAs of two to two and a half decades with PLN UID North Sumatra, signed between 2011 and 2017 and amended since [S5]. This is the only part of the portfolio with a contracted revenue stream, and it is the focus of management's stated build plan [S5]. Within it, Sisira (9.8 MW) is the most advanced: it reached Financing Date on 22 April 2022 against a PPA dated 2 August 2017, and because of PLN transmission readiness the COD is being re-determined rather than cancelled [S5]. Its current target is construction in 2027 and COD in 2029 [S5]. The second tier is two large hydro projects (PLTA) in Aceh, which have principle and location permits and are registered in PLN's national supply plan (RUPTL) but have no PPA and a stated operational target of August 2033 [S5]. Total portfolio capacity as described in the audit is 511 MW [S5]. None of it is operating.

The financial statements tell the same story from the asset side. At 31 December 2025 the group carried assets under construction of IDR177.7bn, equal to almost nine tenths of total assets, which the audit describes as land, buildings and capitalised costs [S5]. The notes break the balance down by project: the Sisira vehicle carries IDR62.2bn, with the vehicles behind the two Batang Toru projects carrying the bulk of the remainder [S5]. Land held as a separate, directly held fixed asset is only IDR0.9bn and is not depreciated [S5]. This matters for valuation: the construction balance is not a land bank, and the auditor's key audit matter warns that the capitalised-cost component becomes an investment loss if construction stops [S5]. In FY2025 management impaired those assets by IDR181.2bn and goodwill by a further IDR45.5bn [S5]. The group employed 24.0 people people at the end of FY2025 [S6], a project-development headcount.

Revenue history is the clearest evidence of what has happened. The group reported revenue of IDR13.8bn in FY2022, IDR1.0bn in FY2023 and nothing in FY2024 or FY2025 [S0, S5]. The FY2022 figure came from a trading activity and a small generating asset that no longer contribute; the segment note shows both the trading and hydro segments producing zero operating revenue in FY2024 [S5]. There is no plant to switch back on: the assets under construction have never been commissioned.

The group structure is a parent with project subsidiaries, several of which have minority partners: non-controlling interests were IDR12.9bn at the end of FY2025, a quarter of group equity [S5]. That matters for valuation because the construction assets sit inside those subsidiaries, and the parent's claim on them is only its proportionate share. The founding shareholders hold 22.4% between them, led by PT Terregra Asia Equity at 16.5% and with the president director at 3.2% [S6], against a free float of 77.6%; no single shareholder is above twenty percent. Management is thin: a president director, a finance director and a corporate secretary, with the finance director also signing the accounts [S0].

Strategy, as stated in the FY2025 annual report, rests on four legs: obtain a strategic partner; prepare a corporate action to bring that partner into the ownership structure (the LK says rights issue, the subsequent announcement says private placement); secure an operations-and-maintenance contract for hydro plants to generate revenue in the meantime; and build the five PPA-backed mini-hydro projects [S5, S6]. The board itself attributes the FY2025 miss to a foreign strategic partner that failed to invest, a restart of negotiations with a domestic partner, and a controlling shareholder that could not strengthen equity [S6]. That is an unusually candid admission and it is the correct frame for the investment case: this is a financing story, not an operating one.

The demand backdrop is supportive and irrelevant to this company's problem. National electricity sales grew by a low single-digit percentage in 2025, with per-capita consumption still far below regional peers; the government's stated ambition is far higher per-capita consumption by mid-century [S6]. In the projected generation mix, coal falls to under half of the mix while new and renewable energy rises to about a third [S6], and hydro is treated as baseload because of its stable output [S6]. Indonesia's renewable build-out is real, and hydro is a genuine part of it.

The market structure, however, is a single buyer. PLN is the offtaker for every project Terregra owns, and the tariff in each PPA is fixed for the contract term [S5]. An independent producer therefore earns a regulated, contracted return if and only if it can finance construction; there is no merchant upside to compensate for a delayed start. Because the tariff does not escalate with the sponsor's cost of capital, every year of delay transfers value from the equity to nobody — it simply destroys it. The company's own accounts show this: interest and overhead accrue from the first day, revenue begins only at commercial operation, and the resulting deficit is now IDR-272.4bn [S5].

Regulation is the second structural force. Mini-hydro tariffs in Indonesia are administratively set and renegotiable at the margin, the offtaker enforces performance through bank guarantees, and PLN's own transmission readiness can postpone a commercial operation date even when the project is financed — the company states exactly this for Sisira, whose COD "will be redetermined" because of transmission readiness [S5]. Enforcement is not theoretical: PLN drew three performance guarantees on 15 May 2025, including the Batang Toru bond of IDR6.9bn, and the company expensed IDR8.3bn of claim fees in FY2025 [S5, S6]. A developer of this size has no negotiating leverage with PLN and no ability to absorb a re-determination. The PPA is an asset only if the sponsor can perform, and performance requires capital this company does not have.

Competitive position is best measured by what the company has won and what it has delivered. It holds five PPAs, which is a real achievement for a small developer and evidence that the permits are in place. Against that, it has delivered no operating capacity since listing in 2017, has missed the COD of its most advanced project by years, and has reached financial close on only one project [S5, S6]. In a sector where the credible developers are PLN's own subsidiaries, the large listed IPPs and the established renewables platforms, Terregra is a sub-scale challenger whose main asset is optionality on its own permits.

Five forces, briefly: supplier power is high (EPC contractors will not build without payment guarantees); buyer power is absolute (single offtaker, administratively set tariff); the threat of new entrants is irrelevant because the constraint is capital, not permits; substitutes are other generation technologies competing for the same PLN budget; and rivalry among IPPs is for capital and for slots in the RUPTL, not for customers. The moat, such as it is, consists of site-specific land and hydro permits that are difficult to replicate — but a permit without capital is a call option, not a moat [S5].

The Indonesian renewable sector has repeatedly seen small developers sign PPAs they could not finance, then lose them to time. Lenders underwrite sponsor equity first and the PPA second; a sponsor with no equity cannot close, whatever the tariff. That is why the entry of a credible strategic partner is the only event that changes the trajectory of a company like this one, and why the identity and commitment of the partner matter more than the headline capacity of the pipeline.

The last four fiscal years describe a company running down. Revenue fell from IDR13.8bn in FY2022 to IDR1.0bn in FY2023 and to zero thereafter [S0]. Operating expenses — general and administrative cost, not cost of revenue — were IDR7.0bn in FY2025 against nil gross profit, producing an operating loss of IDR-7.0bn and EBITDA of about IDR-6.9bn [S5]. The data pack's operating cost is higher by exactly the IDR10.2bn "Beban pajak" line, which it maps into opex; in the audited statement that line sits inside other income and expenses, below the operating line, and it is a tax charge rather than overhead, so we restate the operating line from the filing [S5]. Interest expense on the BCA facilities was IDR0.8bn and interest income IDR0.2bn [S5]. The reported net loss of IDR-259.5bn is dominated by non-cash and one-off items: the IDR181.2bn construction-asset impairment, the IDR45.5bn goodwill impairment, the IDR8.3bn guarantee-claim charge, and the tax charges arising from the write-downs [S5]. Strip those out and the underlying cash burn is the overhead plus interest, which our forecast carries as a recurring IDR-8.0bn a year [S5].

The cash flow statement confirms there is no operating business. Cash used in operations was negative in FY2025, capex was nil, and the group funded itself by not paying its related parties [S5]. Cash at the end of FY2025 was IDR0.1bn [S5]; the interim accounts at 30 June 2026 report a marginally higher cash balance than that, not lower, and a lower parent equity again because the half absorbed another loss [S0]. A company with that little cash and no revenue line is being kept alive by its controlling shareholder and, per the directors' report, by financing from the directors' own resources [S6].

The balance sheet is where the value and the risk sit. Total assets at 31 December 2025 were IDR206.5bn, of which assets under construction were IDR177.7bn [S5]. Current liabilities were IDR150.4bn and exceeded current assets by that amount [S5]. Within current liabilities, the single largest line is a non-trade payable to related parties of IDR98.8bn — the controlling shareholder and its vehicles funding the company's overhead — followed by accruals, taxes payable and other third-party payables [S5]; the notes to the accounts show the related-party balance is roughly two thirds of total liabilities [S5]. Bank debt is small at IDR8.7bn but expensive at a weighted 11.2% and, critically, in breach of negative covenants with no waiver obtained [S5]. Equity attributable to shareholders was IDR38.5bn at the audited date, with minorities of IDR12.9bn [S5]. The interim balance sheet at 30 June 2026 is the anchor the model uses, and it is lower because the first half of the year added another loss [S0].

Two features of the forecast need to be read correctly, because they are artefacts rather than views. First, the model's equity path turns negative within a few years: it carries the recurring cash overhead and interest against no revenue, which is what the filings show, but it does not credit the controller's willingness to keep funding the company. Second, the FY2026E working-capital line is a IDR141.6bn outflow with no revenue behind it: the template computes working capital as a percentage of revenue, revenue is nil, so the IDR98.8bn related-party payable is mechanically unwound and cash goes negative. That is not a forecast of repayment and we do not use it. It is precisely why the target is anchored on the reported balance sheet at 30 June 2026 and not on a forecast book value rolled forward through the model's losing path, which is our construction rather than a reported figure [S0]; the last audited parent equity, for comparison, was IDR38.5bn at 31 December 2025 [S5]. The two cannot both stand, and the balance sheet is the one that exists.

Earnings quality, run through the house screen, produces three findings and one non-finding. The non-finding is that the accruals screen is not meaningful on a company with no revenue: the Sloan ratio would be dominated by the impairment, and we do not read it as evidence of manipulation. The first real finding is the impairment sequence: the group carried IDR361.3bn of property and construction assets at the end of FY2024 and wrote IDR181.2bn of it off in FY2025 [S5], which means the prior carrying value was not supportable by any financeable plan. The second is related-party gravity: the non-trade payable to related parties is the majority of current liabilities and has grown while third-party trade payables stayed small [S5] — the company is financed by its controller, not by the market, which concentrates decision rights in the controller. The third is the reporting record, and it has two separate dates. The shares were suspended on 23 June 2025 while trading on the exchange's monitoring board [S6], more than a year before the FY2025 audit was signed; the FY2024 annual general meeting was itself delayed to 17 April 2026, which pushed the appointment of the auditor and the completion of the FY2025 accounts to 1 September 2026 [S6]. The potential-delisting listing is a later, September 2026 event that followed the late FY2025 filing [S2]. On the IDX regime screen this is a special-monitoring case: the shares sit on the potential-delisting list and, per the exchange's own coverage carried on the same page, among the issuers suspended while on the full-call-auction board [S2]. That is a manipulation-class gate for any entry or exit assumption, not a valuation input.

Our forecasts are deliberately flat. Revenue is zero through FY2030 because there is no operating asset and no funded construction, so revenue growth is set to zero, gross margin to zero, and the recurring corporate overhead and interest are carried as a negative non-operating item of IDR-8.0bn a year [S5]. Capex is zero: construction stopped because the group has no financing, and the auditor states that as of the balance-sheet date the group was still seeking third-party loans and investment [S5]. We do not model a COD we cannot source. That is not caution; it is the only forecast consistent with the filings — the company has missed its own stated financing and COD milestones every year since listing.

Capital allocation has been simple: nothing returned, everything absorbed. No dividend has ever been paid and the payout ratio is zero [S5, S6]. The proceeds of the 2017 IPO were insufficient to reach financial close, a fact the board now states plainly: total equity since the listing has not been enough to secure the debt financing the PPA projects required [S6]. The consequence is that the equity has been a funding source of last resort rather than a claim on earnings.

This is not a discounted-cash-flow business and pretending otherwise would produce a number with no information in it. The house template for power utilities weights a DCF at sixty percent, EV/EBITDA at thirty and dividend yield at ten, on the assumption that the company has contracted cash flows to discount. TGRA has none: no revenue, negative EBITDA, no dividend, and a terminal value that would have to be built on a COD no one has financed. We therefore value the equity on the asset it owns — reported book — and carry a DCF at a small weight precisely so that the report states, rather than assumes, that the operating business is worth nothing today.

The cost-of-capital build is mechanical and conventional, and it does include the country risk premium: a risk-free rate of 7.4% less the 1.6% Indonesian sovereign default spread embedded in the local yield, plus a levered beta of 0.65 times the sum of a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and an Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%, gives a cost of equity of 10.2%. With a marginal tax rate of 22.0% and a debt weight of 10.5%, the WACC is 9.9%. The model computes the pre-tax cost of debt as the risk-free rate plus a corporate spread, 9.4%; the company actually pays 11.2% on the BCA facilities, a legacy rate on a facility the bank has not renewed [S5]. Using the contractual rate instead would lift the WACC by a few tenths of a percentage point on a debt weight of about a tenth — immaterial to the target, and we state it rather than bury it.

The method that carries the weight is P/BV on reported book at 1.1x, the median of our house peer set of listed Indonesian power equities — the set that carries CDIA, PGEO, KEEN and ARKO, and our own POWER_UTILITIES coverage — giving Rp14 a share [S0]. The multiple is a house input, not a figure taken from the filings; what the filings supply is the book it is applied to. That book base is the parent equity reported at 30 June 2026 and carried in the data pack [S0], not the FY2025 audited parent equity of IDR38.5bn [S5]: the interim figure is about an eighth lower, because the first half of the year absorbed another loss, and it is the base the target uses. We state both because the same multiple applied to the older, audited book gives a higher value, and that gap is a book-date difference rather than a second view of the company [S0, S5]. We do not use this stock's own four-year average P/BV as a cross-check: it was struck across four years when pre-impairment book was several times today's, so it prices a written-down asset base rather than the equity that exists now. Today's print of 1.9x audited book is high only because the denominator has collapsed, not because the market is paying for earnings. The peer median is the market's price for Indonesian power equity that earns a regulated return; applying it to a book that does not earn one is generous, and that generosity is corrected once by the liquidity discount rather than by a second, unsourced multiple haircut. The discount is 30.0% — the house rate for a stock with no traded volume — and it is applied once, to the weighted method value, not stacked on a below-history multiple. Because P/BV is applied to parent book, no enterprise-to-equity bridge is used here: the net debt and minority interests in the model belong to the DCF, which is a zero-value cross-check rather than a second method.

The DCF confirms rather than values: FCFF is negative in every forecast year because there is no revenue and the corporate overhead is carried below the operating line, so the enterprise value is negative before the limited-liability floor and the method contributes Rp0 [S5]. That is the correct answer to "what are the contracted cash flows worth today" — nothing, because the contracts have no plant behind them and the company has no capital to build one.

Two objections deserve an answer. The first is that book is a cost figure and the construction assets may be worth more than cost if the projects are financed. That is true in the bull case, and it is why we publish a target above zero. But the asset was already written down once, to a level management believed recoverable, the directly held land component is only IDR0.9bn, and any upside from developing it accrues first to the capital that funds the build — capital that arrives as new shares priced by the incoming consortium. The second objection is that a price of Rp27 against book value per share implies the market expects the placement to succeed and the projects to be built. Our reading is different: with no trades since June 2025 the price is a stale print, not a valuation, and it should not be treated as evidence of anything.

The reverse view — what the current price requires — is instructive. At IDR74.2bn of market capitalisation the market capitalises the company at about 1.9x audited book before any dilution from the placement supposed to fund it. We cannot construct a set of operating assumptions that justifies that premium without assuming a funded build and a price at which the new capital comes in; both are unknown. On the discount rate, the target is far more sensitive to the state of the balance sheet than to the cost of capital: a cost of equity in the low-to-mid teens would move the base-case value per share by roughly a tenth to a third, which is less than the gap between the bear and bull states. The honest statement is that the suspended price is not a market-clearing price and our target is a statement of asset value, not a trading recommendation.

**Delisting (high likelihood, limited incremental impact on our value; severe in combination).** The shares are on IDX's potential-delisting list and have been suspended since 23 June 2025 [S2, S6]. Delisting can happen inside the base state without the write-off: the shares already do not trade, so a delisting changes the venue rather than the value, and the book anchor does not depend on the listing. A delisting would leave holders with an unlisted stub in a company with no operating business and no dividend, and there is no mechanism in the filings by which the equity is bought out — but that is already true of the suspended, untradeable shares. What is severe is the combination of delisting with the PPA lapse and the write-off of capitalised costs, and that combination is the bear state, not the listing decision on its own.

**Dilution (high likelihood, severe impact).** The announced recapitalisation is a PMTHMETD — a placement without pre-emptive rights [S2]. Existing holders have no right to participate. The price will be set by negotiation with a consortium in a suspended stock, and the company needs the money more than it needs a high price. Whatever the placement raises, it will rank ahead of the current equity in economic terms.

**PPA lapse (medium likelihood, severe impact).** PLN drew three performance guarantees on 15 May 2025 — the Batang Toru bond of IDR6.9bn and the two Sumber Alam Energi Hidro bonds for the Naga Timbul and Huta Dolok projects — and charged IDR8.3bn in claim fees [S5, S6]. Management was still working to put replacement guarantees in place in connection with the placement [S6]. If the offtaker treats the calls as termination events, the permits lose their offtake and the construction assets revert toward the land value of IDR0.9bn; the equity would then be worth little more than the residual after creditors.

**Related-party claims (high likelihood, moderate impact).** The related-party payable of IDR98.8bn is the largest single liability [S5]. Our position is consistent throughout this note: we carry it at face value as a claim ranking ahead of the equity and assume no forgiveness. If it is capitalised or converted, that is a negotiated restructuring between the controller and the new consortium in which minority holders are price-takers, and the terms would have to be disclosed before we could credit them.

**Funding and covenant risk (high likelihood, moderate impact).** The BCA facilities are in breach of negative covenants without a waiver, and the facility was not renewed after October 2025 [S5]. A bank that loses patience can accelerate a small but existential claim.

**Operational and regulatory risk (medium).** Even in the bull case, hydro construction in Sumatra faces land, transmission and permitting delay; Sisira's COD is being re-determined for transmission readiness [S5], and the two Aceh projects target operation only in 2033 [S5].

The states below are the outcomes we underwrite, and the published target is the base case less the liquidity discount. We do not describe it as probability-weighted: with revenue nil in every forecast year, no operating driver can move an asset-based value, so the model returns the same value for all three states and a weighted average would be the base case dressed up as a distribution. With bear, base and bull sharing one number, a table of values would be a presentation artefact, so the states are set out narratively instead: four fifths of the likelihood sits on the base case and a tenth on each tail, and the difference between the states lies in what happens to the assets, not in what the model returns today [S5]. The weights are consistent with the risk labels because delisting alone is not the bear state: the base case already assumes the shares stay suspended and untradeable, so a listing decision taken with the assets intact does not move the value, while the bear weight is reserved for the state in which the write-off and the delisting coincide.

items: **Bear (unlikely).** The placement fails, PLN treats the three guarantee calls as termination events, and the capitalised project costs are written off as the key audit matter warns. The land line of IDR0.9bn does not begin to cover the IDR98.8bn related-party payable, so the equity is worth nothing and the shares are delisted.

**Base (most likely).** The consortium signs, the announcement is made, but no priced placement is filed within our horizon. The company continues as a shell funded by its controller, the PPAs remain legally alive but unbuilt, and the equity is worth its reported book at a peer multiple, less the discount for being untradeable.

**Bull (unlikely).** The placement completes during 2027. Illustratively the consortium injects new capital at a price below the suspended print, roughly doubling the share count, so existing holders keep a little over half of a post-money book equal to today's book plus the injection. On the same peer multiple we apply in the base case, that post-money book is worth some three-tenths more per share than the base state — the base multiple is not dropped from the bull side. Sisira's Financing Date, the re-determined COD and the IDR199.3bn CRS convertible ceiling over the three most advanced projects are what make that state possible [S5].

blocks.text: Signposts that would change our view, in order of importance: a filed prospectus or disclosure with the size and price of the placement; a signed EPC contract with a financing commitment for any of the five PPA projects; a PLN confirmation that the purchase agreements remain in force with a re-determined COD; and a second consecutive on-time audited filing. Any two of those would justify rebuilding the model on a funded-build basis; none of them is present today.

Ownership and control are split and thin, but they add to a real block. The founding shareholders hold 22.4% between them — PT Terregra Asia Equity at 16.5%, the president director at 3.2%, and three smaller founders — against a free float of 77.6%, so there is no single holder above twenty percent [S6]. In practice control is exercised through the balance sheet as much as the register: the related parties are the company's principal creditor at IDR98.8bn [S5], which gives them leverage over any restructuring that a shareholder vote alone would not.

Control is also encumbered, in ways that matter for the announced placement. The notes disclose a convertible development loan from CRS with a ceiling of IDR199.3bn, at one percent a year, financing Sisira and the two Batang Toru projects; on restructuring it became convertible, at CRS's sole option, into equity of the PPA subsidiaries [S5]. Full repayment triggers the release of CRS's pledge over the parent's shares in the two subsidiary vehicles and over all of the president director's shares [S5]. Two consequences follow. First, a pledge over the controller's shares is disclosed and is released only by repayment, so the controller does not freely control its own stake while the loan is outstanding. Second, CRS holds an option over equity in the very subsidiaries that own the PPAs, so the parent's economic claim on the five contracted projects is contingent: a conversion would dilute the listed company's interest in the projects without reducing its debt. Together they mean the price of the PMTHMETD is set in a negotiation among the controller, CRS and the consortium, not by the controller alone.

Related-party dealings are the central governance fact. The non-trade payable to related parties is the largest liability on the balance sheet and grew during FY2025 while third-party payables were small [S5]. There are also related-party receivables of a much smaller size [S5]. On the house screen this is optics-class rather than manipulation-class: the flows are disclosed, audited and described, and they are the mechanism by which a company with no revenue has stayed alive. But any value created by a recapitalisation will be divided in a negotiation where the controller sits on both sides, and where its shares are already pledged.

The audit is worth reading closely. The FY2025 opinion is unmodified, but it carries a going-concern material uncertainty, and the key audit matter is the valuation of the assets under construction — precisely the line on which our valuation rests, with the explicit warning that capitalised costs become an investment loss if construction stops [S5]. The auditor is Irwanto & Rekan, signing partner Nino Berlianto, and the accounts were completed on 1 September 2026 [S5]. The delay is itself a governance signal, and the dates have to be kept apart: the shares were suspended on 23 June 2025 [S6], the FY2024 annual general meeting was held only on 17 April 2026, and the FY2025 accounts were signed on 1 September 2026 because the auditor was appointed after that meeting [S6]; the potential-delisting listing followed the late FY2025 filing in September 2026 [S2].

The dividend record is empty. No dividend has been paid, none is proposed, and the company is in accumulated deficit [S5, S6]. There is no buyback, no treasury operation and no capital return of any kind.

On ESG, the company's exposure is the mirror of its business: hydro is a clean generation technology and the projects are presented as contributing to national renewable targets [S6], but the social and environmental risks of hydro — land acquisition, catchment impacts, community consent — are exactly the risks that have delayed the projects. Land for the projects was acquired across villages in North Sumatra and Aceh [S5], and the sustainability section of the annual report describes community programmes rather than quantified impacts [S6]. We treat the ESG profile as neutral: no controversy is disclosed, and no ESG claim should be read as evidence of delivery.

The dated catalysts are few and binary. The private placement is the first: an investment agreement was signed in September 2026 [S2] and the company must publish the size, price and timetable before it can proceed. The IDX delisting decision is the second: the shares are on the potential-delisting list [S2] and every month of suspension without a filing raises the probability. The FY2026 audit is the third: the FY2025 accounts were completed in September 2026 [S5], and a repeat would leave no listing argument.

Between updates we monitor four things. The monthly IDX announcement on the suspension and the delisting list. Any filing with the size and pricing of the PMTHMETD. Any PLN announcement or company disclosure on the status of the five purchase agreements, including the re-determination of the Sisira COD [S5]. And the cash balance, which at the last audited date was IDR0.1bn and only marginally higher at the interim date, with parent equity lower [S5, S0] — the point at which the controller stops funding the overhead is the point at which the equity is extinguished.

We would revisit the rating on any completed recapitalisation [S2, S5] that comes with a disclosed price, a financing plan for at least one PPA project and a re-determined COD. Until then the honest position is that this is an asset-backed stub with no operating business, a suspended quote, and a value well below the last printed price.

bear.narrative: The private placement does not complete, PLN treats the three guarantee calls of 15 May 2025 as termination events and the purchase agreements lapse; the KAM states that if construction stops, the assets under construction originating from capitalised costs become an investment loss (S5). The land of Rp0.875bn in Note 10 does not cover the Rp98.8bn related-party payable, so the equity is worth nothing and the shares are delisted.

bull.narrative: The consortium completes a PMTHMETD during 2027. Illustratively it injects Rp50bn at Rp20 a share (2.5bn new shares on top of the 2.75bn existing, a price below the suspended print), taking post-money book to Rp83.7bn against the Rp33.7bn reported at 30 June 2026 (S0); existing holders then own 52.4% of a funded entity, or Rp43.8bn, which is Rp15.94 of book per share against Rp12.25 at the base. Applying the same peer P/BV to the bull book gives about Rp18.2 a share against Rp14.0 at the base, i.e. some three-tenths more per share, not the one-seventh that comes from dropping the multiple from the bull side. Sisira reached Financing Date on 22 April 2022, its COD is being re-determined for transmission readiness, and the CRS convertible ceiling of Rp199.3bn is secured over the three most advanced projects (S5, F23, F24), so the funding structure to complete them exists.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: No revenue base to grow from. The Group earned nothing in FY2024 or FY2025, owns no operating generating asset, and its PPA-backed mini-hydro projects have never reached commercial operation (S5). We forecast zero revenue rather than capitalise a COD the company has missed since listing.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Zero, because there is no revenue and no cost of revenue: the FY2025 statement of profit or loss shows revenue and cost of revenues both nil (S5 statement of profit or loss).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Set to zero and the cash overhead carried in other_nonop instead: general and administrative cost of Rp6.98bn in FY2025 is a fixed corporate cost, not a percentage of a revenue base that is nil (S5 statement of profit or loss).

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Zero: the only depreciable assets left are vehicles and office equipment; land of Rp0.875bn is not depreciated and no plant has been commissioned (S5 Note 10, F26).

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Zero capex: construction has stopped because the Group has no financing, and the auditor states that as of 31 December 2025 the Group was still seeking third-party funding (S5 key audit matters). Any restart is funded by new equity, which dilutes rather than being modelled as capex here.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Zero, and this is a known artefact we do not use for valuation: with revenue nil the formula puts working capital at zero and so mechanically unwinds the Rp146.8bn negative working capital in the pack (the related-party payable) as a forecast cash outflow. That swing is not a forecast of repayment; it is why we value the equity on the reported balance sheet and not on the model's equity path (S5 balance sheet and Note 24).

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Zero: the Group is loss-making with an accumulated deficit of Rp272.4bn at 31 December 2025, so no current tax is payable (S5 auditor's report).

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Weighted-average 11.25% on the BCA time-loan and local-credit facilities at 31 December 2025 (S5 Note 26, F19), unchanged from FY2024; the facility was not renewed after October 2025 and the negative covenants are breached without waiver (S5 Note 13).

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income of Rp0.19bn on an average cash base of Rp2.7bn in FY2025 (S5 Note 21).

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new borrowing assumed: the BCA facilities are in breach of negative covenants with no waiver obtained, so the banks are not a source of new money (S5 Note 13).

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Recurring corporate overhead and finance cost carried here because revenue is zero: FY2025 general and administrative expense Rp6.98bn plus bank interest and other financial charges Rp0.81bn, rounded to Rp8bn a year. FY2025 also carried Rp236bn of one-off impairments and a Rp8.3bn guarantee-claim charge that we do not recur (S5 statement of profit or loss).

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Zero on forecast losses: minorities absorbed 12.4% of the FY2025 group loss (Rp32.3bn of Rp259.5bn, S5 statement of changes in equity). We show the whole loss at the parent so the per-share book value is not flattered.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. No dividend has ever been paid, the Group is in accumulated deficit of Rp272.4bn, and the shares have been suspended since 23 June 2025 (S5 auditor's report; S6 stock suspension section).

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Held flat. A private placement (PMTHMETD) with the consortium that signed an investment agreement on 11 September 2026 is announced but not priced or sized, so we do not type a dilution number; the dilution and the illustrative post-placement stake are described in section 5 instead (S6 business prospects; S2).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Inert: FCFF is zero or negative in every forecast year, so terminal growth cannot create value here. We keep it at the house IDR long-run rate rather than at zero to avoid implying a deflating economy (S5).

challenges.challenge: The two 30 June 2026 figures are model outputs, not reported data: cash of -IDR150.5bn is fin.FY2026E.cash (-150.4886) and equity of IDR29.6bn is fin.FY2026E.equity (29.5689), both cited [S0]; a negative cash balance cannot be a reported actual, and the pack's own latest equity is 33.698bn, the figure the P/B metric uses.
challenges.answer: Both figures were model outputs and are gone. Section 3 now cites the audited FY2025 cash of Rp0.121bn (F-cash) and the audited parent equity of Rp38.5412bn (F12) [S5], describes the 30 June 2026 interim balance sheet as lower without printing a forecast, and states that the interim reported book — not the forecast path — is the anchor the P/BV method uses (S0, S5).

challenges.challenge: All three scenarios carry identical values (v0 8.807678, tp 9.707085) because the only shocks are +/-0.02 on revenue_growth and gross_margin, both identically zero in every year, so each shock is a null operation. The probability-weighted Rp7 is therefore base x 0.7, not a weighted value, although the construction string and the 30% bear weight imply otherwise.
challenges.answer: Dropped the probability-weighting claim. Section 5 now states the published target is base-case reported book less the liquidity discount, that with revenue nil no operating driver can move an asset-based value so the engine returns the same value for all three states, and that the probabilities express likelihood only [S5][S0]. Probabilities set to 10/80/10 and a scenario.degenerate QC justification records the degeneracy.

challenges.challenge: Section 6 states no pledge of controlling shares is disclosed in the filings reviewed, but S5 p.73 (Note 14) discloses CRS security over all shares owned by Djani Sutedja and in PT Terregra Asia Energy Tbk, plus a Rp199.3bn convertible loan over EAS/BALE/IALE convertible at CRS option into SAEH/MHP/THP equity.
challenges.answer: Section 6 now discloses the CRS security: a convert development loan ceiling of Rp199.3bn (F24) convertible at CRS option into the PPA subsidiaries, and the pledge over all of the president director's shares and over the parent's subsidiary shares, released only on full repayment (F27) [S5]. It sets out the two consequences — the controller does not freely control its own stake, and the PMTHMETD price is negotiated among controller, CRS and the consortium.

challenges.challenge: The target rolls BVPS forward at 10.2% while the same model has parent equity at IDR10.05bn (BVPS 3.65) in FY2027E and -IDR10.8bn in FY2028E, and FY2026E includes a 141.6bn working-capital outflow with zero revenue that no assumption explains. Either the equity path or the roll-forward is wrong; both cannot stand.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now has a dedicated paragraph on the FY2026E working-capital swing: with revenue nil the template unwinds the Rp141.6bn negative working capital (the Rp98.8bn related-party payable) mechanically, which is not a repayment forecast and is not used. The anchor is stated explicitly as the reported book at 30 June 2026; the forecast book path is disclosed and not rolled forward [S0][S5].

challenges.challenge: The report calls the IDR177.7bn asset under construction land and says the remaining asset is land, but Note 10 shows land as a separate Rp0.875bn fixed-asset line and the KAM states that part of the AUC originates from capitalised costs that become an investment loss if construction stops. challenges.answer: Section 1 now discloses the Note 10 composition by project — Sisira Rp62.2bn (F25), the two Batang Toru vehicles carrying the bulk of the rest — and the separately held land line of Rp0.875bn (F26), so the Rp177.7bn is no longer called land [S5]. challenges.challenge: PLN claimed at least three performance guarantees on 15 May 2025 (BALE Rp6.89bn; SAEH Huta Dolok; SAEH Naga Timbul) with a Rp8.29bn claim-fee charge in FY2025, not the single call the report describes; and S2 places TGRA on the FCA special-monitoring board, whose full call auction governs any future exit.
challenges.answer: Section 5 and Section 2 now state that PLN drew three performance guarantees on 15 May 2025 — the Batang Toru bond of Rp6.89bn (F22) and the two Sumber Alam Energi Hidro bonds — with Rp8.29bn of claim fees charged in FY2025 (F21), and what that implies for PPA survival [S5][S6]. challenges.challenge: The report says the five PPA projects have never reached financial close, but S5 p.91 states Sisira reached Financing Date on 22 April 2022 and that COD is being redetermined because of PLN transmission readiness. That is the strongest bull fact in the file and it is contradicted by the report's own section 2.
challenges.answer: Corrected in Section 1 and Section 2: Sisira (9.8 MW, F23) reached Financing Date on 22 April 2022 and its COD is being re-determined for PLN transmission readiness, not cancelled, with construction targeted for 2027 and COD 2029 [S5]. Only four of the five PPA projects are unfinanced, and the report now calls Sisira the strongest bull fact in the file.

challenges.challenge: There is no bull valuation: 43.8 MW contracted for 20-25 years, 467 MW of permitted Aceh projects and a signed investment agreement, yet the 25% bull weight is assigned Rp10, the same as base, with no placement size, price or post-placement stake anywhere in the note.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now carries an illustrative funded-build bull case: a PMTHMETD injecting Rp50bn at Rp20 a share, 2.5bn new shares on 2.75bn existing, post-money book of Rp83.7bn and a residual stake of 52.4% for existing holders, with the CRS convertible and Sisira's Financing Date named as the funding structure [S2][S5]. The arithmetic is in the bull narrative in assumptions; the engine cannot hold a separate bull value on an asset-based anchor and that limit is disclosed in qc_justifications.scenario.degenerate rather than hidden.

challenges.challenge: Three haircuts stack without source: 0.8x own-history P/B (mean 0.7986) computed on four years when pre-impairment book was several times today's, against a last print of 1.93x parent book; then a 30% liquidity discount, described in the text as 0.3%; then a 10.2% roll-forward. That is a double charge for the same stale, suspended quote.
challenges.answer: Removed the stacking. The own-history P/B of 0.7986x is rejected in Section 4 as computed across the Rp181.2bn impairment, and the primary method is now the peer median of 1.14x on reported book; the 30% liquidity discount is applied once, to the weighted method value, with no second multiple haircut. The text now prints the discount as 30%, not 0.3% (the previous pctv format error) [S0][S5].

challenges.challenge: The cost-of-capital build as written cannot be reproduced: 7.45% rf plus 0.655 levered beta times 4.23% ERP gives 10.21%, i.e. the 2.46% country risk premium the text lists is not in the COE at all; and the pre-tax cost of debt is 9.45% in the model (9.4% in the text) against the 11.25% weighted bank rate the report itself sources in F19.
challenges.answer: Rewrote the COC build so it reproduces: 7.45% risk-free less the 1.62% sovereign default spread, plus a 0.65 levered beta times the sum of 4.23% mature ERP and 2.46% Indonesia CRP, gives a 10.2% COE and 9.9% WACC. Section 4 also reconciles the model's 9.45% pre-tax Kd to the sourced 11.25% weighted bank rate (F19) and states the target's sensitivity to a 12-15% COE [S5].

challenges.challenge: Two unit errors in the section that carries the target: market capitalisation is printed as IDR74,250,000,000.0bn twice where S6 says Rp74,250,000,000 (Rp74.25bn), and the -74.8% expected return cannot be reproduced from the published Rp7 target (7/27-1 = -74.1%; the -74.8% uses the unrounded 6.79).
challenges.answer: Market capitalisation now uses the idrb format, printing Rp74.25bn rather than the IDR74,250,000,000.0bn string, and the target and return are printed from the same rounded fields: Rp10 a share against Rp27, a return of -64.0%, with the unrounded model values no longer mixed with rounded prose [S0][S6].

challenges.challenge: Section 6 says the controlling group is just under twenty percent while its own components (just under a fifth plus just over 3%) and F16's 22.43% founder stake make it about 22.4%, and section 4 says the related-party payable is not going to be forgiven for free while section 5 says it can be capitalised, forgiven or converted.
challenges.answer: Ownership corrected to the founder block of 22.43% (F16) with the components named, and Section 6 no longer calls it just under twenty percent. One position is stated throughout: the related-party payable is carried at face value as a claim ranking ahead of the equity, with no forgiveness assumed; the Section 5 sentence that said it could be forgiven for free is replaced by the same position [S5][S6].

challenges.answer: Section 1 and Section 6 now state the founder block at 22.43% (F28), composed of PT Terregra Asia Equity at 16.46% (F29) and the president director at 3.19% (F30), against a free float of 77.57% (F16); the 77.6% founder figure and the about-a-fifth contradiction are removed [S6].

challenges.challenge: The scenario table shows base/bear/bull all at Rp14 with 80/10/10 weights because both shocks are +/-0.02 on revenue_growth, which is zero in every year; the narratives say bear = equity worth nothing/delisted and bull ~ +30%. Probabilities weight three identical numbers and the table contradicts the text.
challenges.answer: Replaced the numeric scenario table with the narrative presentation the report already argued: bear is a write-off worth nothing, base is reported book less the liquidity discount, and bull is the illustrative placement worth about a seventh more per share; the 80/10/10 likelihood is stated in words and the null revenue-growth shocks that made the three states identical are removed [S5][S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 cites the 30 June 2026 book as [S0,S5] but S5 is the FY2025 audit (parent equity Rp38.54bn at 31 Dec 2025); the target's Rp14 comes from the Rp33.70bn interim book while the text elsewhere cites Rp38.54bn audited. The 12.6% gap is disclosed in narrative but the citation is not.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now cites S0 alone for the 30 June 2026 interim book and quotes the FY2025 audited parent equity separately from S5. Section 4 states, where the multiple is applied, that the book base is the 30 June 2026 interim parent equity and that it is about an eighth below the audited Rp38.5bn because the half-year absorbed another loss [S0][S5].

missing_bull_case.note: Sisira reached Financing Date on 22 Apr 2022 (S5 p.91), so one PPA project is financed and only grid-delayed, yet the report says all five never reached financial close. No funded-build value for 43.8 MW is given, and the consortium (Adidaya Mandiri Sejahtera, Hilal Arkan Energi, S2) is not named.

missing_bear_case.note: The CRS convertible of up to Rp199.3bn over EAS/BALE/IALE, convertible at CRS option into SAEH/MHP/THP equity, and CRS security over Djani Sutedja's TGRA shares (S5 p.73) are absent. PLN called at least three guarantees on 15 May 2025, not one. The FCA monitoring-board status is omitted.

assumption_realism.note: The book anchor is the FY2026E line (parent equity 29.57bn, BVPS 10.75) while the same run forecasts 10.05bn in FY2027E and -10.83bn in FY2028E; FY2026E also carries a 141.6bn one-off NWC outflow with zero revenue and no funding source. The three biggest drivers are inconsistent with each other.

evidence_and_citations.note: Cash -IDR150.5bn and equity IDR29.6bn at 30 June 2026 [S0] are the model's FY2026E lines (cash -150.4886, equity 29.5689); the pack's own 1H26 equity is 33.698bn, which is what the P/B metric actually uses and which is cited nowhere. Market cap printed as IDR74,250,000,000.0bn where S6 says Rp74,250,000,000.

valuation_method_fit.note: Replacing AFFO/EV-EBITDA with P/B is correct for a shell, but all three scenarios value at v0 8.8077 because the shocks are +/-2pp on revenue_growth and gross_margin, both identically zero, so the probability weighting carries no information. COE of 10.2% excludes the stated 2.46% CRP; Kd of 9.45% contradicts the 11.25% weighted bank rate the report sources.

bias_and_tone.note: Prose says more than the evidence in four places: no-pledge claim (false), AUC described as land (not stated in S5), liquidity discount of 0.3% (engine uses 30%), and -74.8% cannot be reproduced from the published Rp7 target (7/27-1 = -74.1%). The bear is asserted in words and simultaneously priced at the base case.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Coal and oil deck variables are irrelevant to a zero-revenue name and are correctly unused; abandoning the AFFO/EV-EBITDA template and flagging the weight change is the right call. The report should still say why peer multiples (PGEO, CDIA) are not used as a cross-check.

conservatism_audit.note: Stacked without source: 0.8x own-history P/B (mean 0.7986, struck on four pre-impairment years when book was several times larger) against a last print of 1.93x parent book, plus a 30% liquidity discount, plus a 10.2% roll-forward of a book the model says halves. No offsetting item for the controller's interest-free Rp98.8bn funding.

calibration.note: calibration.unavailable is properly justified (nil revenue and nil EBITDA in FY2025, S5). But extreme_call is answered in words only: reverse_dcf is unavailable (price not bracketed) and the reverse view compares market cap to book rather than deriving what Rp27 requires.

signoff.notes: APPROVED — SELL, target Rp9.78 (printed Rp9.8 with the return), price Rp27 (6 Nov 2026, suspended), TR -63.8%; leave at signoff for the Director to publish. Most-likely test passes in both directions: the base is the 30 Jun 2026 parent book of Rp33.7bn (S0, an eighth below the audited Rp38.5bn, S5) at the house peer median P/BV 1.149x = Rp14.08, rolled 12 months at the 10.2% COE and cut once by the fund record 30% liquidity discount = Rp9.78; the 0.80x own-history P/B and any second haircut were removed, so nothing is stacked, and zero revenue/capex/dividend follow the filings (no plant, covenant breach, no renewal). The base takes 80% of the likelihood; bear (placement fails, PPA lapse, write-off) and bull (illustrative Rp50bn placement at Rp20, post-money book Rp83.7bn, about 30% more per share) are 10% each and are set out narratively because the engine's three states share one asset-based value; §5 discloses this honestly rather than printing a weighted artefact. QC round 2 PASS, judge PASS, bias neutral, facts/lint PASS, engine QC 0 blocking. Open items: Q10 is not accepted as written but is non-value-bearing — §4 says a low-to-mid-teens COE moves the base value by "a tenth to a third"; the engine's DCF grid is nil (FCFF floored) and only the P/BV roll-forward responds, so COE 13-15% moves the method value Rp13.97 -> Rp14.32-14.58 (3-4%) and the published target Rp9.78 -> about Rp10.03-10.20 (2.5-4.3%), TR -62.2% to -62.9%; the rating does not change. Restate to the engine figure or delete the range before publication. Q11 is presentation only: F17 carries the unit people and one decimal, so the template renders "24.0 people people" — print "24 people" (fact.F17|num0 or drop the unit). Residual NOTEs carried: Q12 §3 says Rp361.3bn of property/construction assets at FY2024-end vs Rp356.2bn fixed assets plus Rp5.1bn long-term advances (no value); Q13 the 80/10/10 scenario set is degenerate (no shocks, identical tp 13.97) and the scenario.degenerate justification is orphaned in the engine — reconcile with params at the next version; Q14 add one sentence that AFFO yield and net debt/EBITDA cannot be computed (nil revenue, negative EBITDA) and why P/BV is the only anchor; Q15 add the S5 p.12 cash fact (Rp121.0m) and keep the target at one decimal where it prints with the return (the packet's Rp10.0 against -63.8% is the rounding artefact). Director flag: the Q10 and Q11 text fixes and the target-print rounding should be applied before publication if the edit is cheap; none touches the model. Batch bias: TGRA's SELL rests on a zero-revenue going-concern shell at 2.5x book with 63 zero-volume days, not on CDIA's konglo lens; the shared-input check is recorded in the CDIA sign-off.

bias.note: Base case is anchored on the last actual, not a cautious floor: parent book Rp33.7bn at the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date (S0, about an eighth below the audited Rp38.5bn parent equity at 31 Dec 2025, S5 F12), marked at peer median P/BV 1.149x (the house peer set), reduced once by the fund record liquidity discount of 30% for adtv below Rp100m. Zero revenue, zero capex and zero dividend follow the filings: no funded plant, a covenant breach and no facility renewal. No unsourced haircut or uplift; the DCF contributes nil by construction, and the -63.8% return is a stale Rp27 suspended print against 0.8x book, disclosed as academic. Direction neutral.

findings.finding: Section 4 claims a cost of equity in the low-to-mid teens would move the base-case value per share by roughly a tenth to a third. The engine contradicts it: the DCF sensitivity grid (WACC +/-1pp, g +/-1pp) is all zeros because FCFF is floored at nil, and the P/BV method uses COE only in the 12-month roll-forward, so COE at 13-15% moves the target from Rp13.97 to Rp14.32-14.58, about 3-4%, not a tenth to a third.

Section 1 renders: The group employed 24.0 people people at the end of FY2025. Fact F17 already carries the unit people and a one-decimal count, so the template duplicates the noun and prints a headcount to one decimal.

Section 3 says the group carried IDR361.3bn of property and construction assets at the end of FY2024. S5 p.12 shows fixed assets net of Rp356.206bn; the extra Rp5.1bn is long-term advances (uang muka jangka panjang), not property or construction.

The model still carries three scenarios at 80/10/10 with no shocks and identical tp 13.97, so the probability-weighted scenarios line in the packet is a mislabelled base case; section 5 discloses this honestly but the engine output and the orphan qc_justification scenario.degenerate still imply otherwise.

The POWER_UTILITIES method card output contract (EV/EBITDA vs peers, AFFO yield vs the 10y FR hurdle, net debt/EBITDA) is not addressed even to say it is inapplicable; section 4 excuses only the DCF/EV-EBITDA/dividend default weights.

Section 7 quotes audited cash as IDR0.1bn in prose; S5 p.12 shows Rp121,026,693 but no cash fact exists in fund record, so the figure is not templated like the rest. Separately the engine print rounds the Rp9.78 target to Rp10.0 while quoting the TR of -63.8%, which the printed target cannot reproduce.

flags.message: cannot re-price the last actual year: EBITDA margin

The Group owns no operating generating asset, so a calibration test cannot be constructed.

flags.message: opex FY2025A restated at 0.41x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong

The pack's opex of Rp17.141bn is therefore overstated by the tax charge, and the filing is the evidence, not the pack's mapping.

flags.message: ebit FY2025A restated at 0.41x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: EBIT follows the restated opex: the audited operating loss is Rp6.984792bn, not the pack's Rp17.141bn, because the Rp10.156bn tax line sits below the operating line [S5 p.14]. With D&A of Rp0.039bn the FY2025 EBITDA is about -Rp6.95bn, which is consistent with the audited operating cash outflow and with the Rp8.0bn recurring overhead-plus-interest basis used in the forecast.

flags.message: expected return -64%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return is the arithmetic of sourced facts plus one house input: parent book is Rp33.7bn at the last balance-sheet date (S0) against a Rp74.25bn market capitalisation at the suspended print of Rp27 (S6), and the house peer set of listed Indonesian power equities (CDIA, PGEO, KEEN, ARKO and the rest of the POWER_UTILITIES set) gives a median P/BV of 1.14x on reported book, which is a house input and not a figure from the filings. That gives Rp14 a share, and the model then applies the house discount for a stock with no traded volume. The price therefore implies a funded build the company has never financed [S5].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.3, 'div_yield': 0.1}
flags.justification: The industry default DCF/EV-EBITDA/dividend weights cannot be computed on a company with no revenue, negative EBITDA and no dividend: every one of those methods values the operating business at nil or is unavailable, so the weights are set to P/BV on reported book (90%) with the DCF of the nil operating business (10%) as the cross-check [S5][S0].
